what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Sites should publish primitives so readers can fix pages
sections.para: The next user experience is the one the reader customises, and sites should encourage it by publishing a small JavaScript page API so every fix is one line. The same API serves tests and agents, kept fixes become a better brief than the site could write, and it is the cheapest accessibility. This newsroom now offers six fixes.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: User-customised pages are next, built on site-published primitives
sections.para: A bookmarklet demo was remembered for its interface, not its exploit, and most sites still fight their readers. The next user experience is customised by the user and paid for, so someone keeps it working. A page API makes fixes one line, the kept fixes become the roadmap, and six run on this newsroom.

sections.label: The bookmarklet that out-designed the application
sections.line: My exploit demo was wanted for its interface
sections.para: During a security assessment I found an injection flaw exposing personal data and demonstrated it as a bookmarklet that laid the records out in a quick Bootstrap interface. The business owner cared more about the interface than the vulnerability, because it beat the legacy application she used every day. An afternoon of Bootstrap beat years of the product.

sections.label: Every site still fights its readers
sections.line: Most sites are built for ads, not readers
sections.para: LinkedIn, YouTube and newspapers surround what you came for with feeds, suggestions and clutter, and even the newest AI assistants have interface gaps users could fix in a line of code. Some of it is lack of time, but the best teams could let users change what they need and have not. Nobody's experience is the average.

sections.label: The next user experience is the one the user customises
sections.line: Users should customise their experience and pay for upkeep
sections.para: The next user experience is set by the person reading, and paid for so someone keeps it working through every release. Bookmarklets, Greasemonkey, Tampermonkey, Violentmonkey, Greasy Fork, Stylus, Arc's Boosts and reader modes already do this. But the site is not involved, so they guess its structure, break when it changes, and often need access to every site.

sections.label: Sites should publish the primitives
sections.line: A page API makes every fix one line
sections.para: If a site publishes its primitives, fixes stop guessing and survive markup changes. The SGraph tools already use window.__tools, a tool:ready event and an api.json, and the same API serves Playwright tests and agents. Kept fixes are a better brief than the site could write: this newsroom shipped five themes after a reader texted "Dark mode!".

sections.label: It is the cheapest accessibility there is
sections.line: Publishing primitives is the cheapest route to accessibility
sections.para: Readers need different things, from bigger text to no motion, and a site that builds every variation itself never finishes. Publishing primitives lets each reader build what they need. WCAG 1.4.12, Text Spacing, assumes users change spacing, and the European Accessibility Act has applied to many consumer services since 28 June 2025.

sections.label: How the fixes reach the page
sections.line: Fixes the reader clicks beat extensions with broad access
sections.para: Fixes can arrive as a bookmarklet, a per-site extension using Chrome's activeTab, or a userscript manager that runs on every site it is allowed on. I prefer the first two because the reader is the one who clicks. One small extension per site, loaded locally from a GitHub repository or an encrypted vault, is far easier to trust.

sections.label: It runs here
sections.line: Six fixes now run on this newsroom
sections.para: Fix the page offers reading mode, bigger text, high contrast, text spacing, outline and markdown, each as a button, a bookmarklet and an API call. One file, page-fixes.js, exposes window.__tools.page with list, apply, toggle and reset, remembering choices in the browser. A generic one-line reading mode for any site shows the limit: it has to guess.

sections.label: The brief
sections.line: The plan: a fix library, extensions and paid upkeep
sections.para: Load the page API on every newsroom page, build a community library of versioned fixes, and ship a per-site activeTab extension. Bring the same API to sgit.ai and ruv.sgit.ai, count kept fixes as the roadmap and adopt popular ones into settings. Let Chrome's model in the tab write fixes, and charge to maintain personal ones.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Six fixes on one site, with no extension yet
sections.para: A strict Content Security Policy can block bookmarklets, the six fixes are a start rather than a library, and the per-site extension is designed but not built. The assessment story is from memory with its details left out, and customisation does not replace good defaults. Suggested fixes go to agent@riskmandate.ai.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: the voice memo, specifications and pages cited
sections.para: A voice memo of 17 October 2026, written up by this site's agent, plus the Fix the page tool, page-fixes.js and its api.json. Also the SGraph tools' JS API convention and architect's review, Chrome's activeTab and userScripts documentation, WCAG 2.2 criterion 1.4.12, the European Accessibility Act and earlier newsroom articles.
